rows.statement: Everything you can touch, and the air around you, is made of atoms.
rows.explanation: Solids, liquids and gases are all made of atoms. Even air is.

rows.statement: Light and heat are made of atoms, just like a rock is.
rows.explanation: Light and heat are not matter. They are not made of atoms.

rows.statement: Every atom has a tiny centre called the nucleus, with electrons around it.
rows.explanation: The nucleus sits in the middle and the electrons are around it.

rows.statement: Neutrons have a negative charge.
rows.explanation: Neutrons have no charge. Electrons are the negative ones.

rows.statement: Protons are positive, electrons are negative, and neutrons have no charge.
rows.explanation: These three charges are what each particle of an atom is like.

rows.statement: If an atom gains a neutron, it becomes a different element.
rows.explanation: The number of protons decides the element. A different number of neutrons only makes a different isotope.

rows.statement: The number of protons in an atom tells you which element it is.
rows.explanation: Every carbon atom has 6 protons and every oxygen atom has 8.

rows.statement: An isotope is always radioactive.
rows.explanation: Many isotopes are perfectly stable. An isotope is not automatically radioactive.

rows.statement: Isotopes of one element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
rows.explanation: Same protons means same element. Different neutrons means a different isotope.

rows.statement: Every nucleus is unstable and will change one day.
rows.explanation: Some nuclei stay the same for ever. Only unstable ones can change.

rows.statement: Any dose of radiation is deadly.
rows.explanation: Everyone gets small doses every day. It takes a very large dose in a short time, about 1000 millisieverts, to make people ill.

rows.statement: The average person in the United States gets about 6 millisieverts of radiation a year, and most of it is natural.
rows.explanation: The average is about 6.2 millisieverts a year, and most of it comes from natural background radiation.

rows.statement: Cells in your body are extremely efficient at repairing radiation damage.
rows.explanation: Ionizing radiation can damage the DNA in cells, and cells repair most of that damage.

rows.statement: Radiation is harmless at every dose.
rows.explanation: A very large dose in a short time makes people ill, and low doses can add a small chance of cancer over a lifetime.

rows.statement: A very large dose of radiation in a short time can cause nausea and vomiting within hours.
rows.explanation: About 1000 millisieverts in a short time is the threshold for acute radiation syndrome.

rows.statement: A small dose every day is the same as one large dose.
rows.explanation: Dose rate matters. A low dose, or one spread over a long time, carries less risk because repair is more likely.

rows.statement: Spending less time near a source lowers the dose from it.
rows.explanation: Limiting the time you are exposed reduces the dose from the radiation source.

rows.statement: The dose from a source decreases dramatically as you move away from it.
rows.explanation: Increasing your distance from a source is one of the three ways to lower a dose.

rows.statement: Barriers of lead, concrete or water protect against penetrating gamma rays.
rows.explanation: Shielding puts material between you and the source, and it can greatly reduce the dose.

rows.statement: A person who was exposed to radiation is radioactive.
rows.explanation: Exposure is not contamination. Radiation does not get on or in people.

rows.statement: All radiation is the same.
rows.explanation: Radiation comes in many kinds. Some can knock electrons out of atoms and some cannot.

rows.statement: Radio waves, microwaves and visible light are radiation, but they do not have enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms.
rows.explanation: They are non-ionizing. Ionizing radiation has enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms.

rows.statement: A sheet of paper stops gamma rays.
rows.explanation: Paper stops alpha particles. Gamma rays pass through it and need thick, dense material to be reduced.

rows.statement: Alpha particles cannot get through the outer layer of your skin.
rows.explanation: Alpha particles are heavy and use up their energy over a very short distance.

rows.statement: Radiation can spread onto you and stay on your skin.
rows.explanation: Radiation does not get on or in people. Radioactive contamination, the material itself, is what can spread.

rows.statement: Being near a source of radiation is not the same as being contaminated.
rows.explanation: Exposure stops when the source is shielded or you move away. Contamination means radioactive material is on or in you.

rows.statement: A Geiger counter that clicks must be next to a radioactive source.
rows.explanation: Background radiation is always around, so a counter picks up some even with no source nearby.

rows.statement: A dosimeter is used to find out how much radiation a person has been exposed to.
rows.explanation: Dosimeters are worn to measure personal exposure.

rows.statement: The becquerel, the gray and the sievert all measure the same thing.
rows.explanation: The becquerel counts decays, the gray measures energy absorbed, and the sievert measures potential for harm.

rows.statement: One becquerel is one decay per second.
rows.explanation: The becquerel measures how active a source is.

rows.statement: Radioactivity is something people invented in the last hundred years.
rows.explanation: Radioactivity was here long before people. It is a natural process.

rows.statement: Rocks, air, food and even your own body contain a little natural radioactivity.
rows.explanation: Natural radioactivity is all around us, and inside us.

rows.statement: Radioactive always means dangerous.
rows.explanation: It depends on the kind and the amount. Radioactive does not automatically mean dangerous.

rows.statement: An unstable nucleus changes all by itself, and nobody can say exactly when one nucleus will change.
rows.explanation: The change is natural and unpredictable for a single nucleus.

rows.statement: An unstable nucleus has to be hit by something before it can decay.
rows.explanation: Natural decay needs no push. The nucleus changes on its own.

rows.statement: Alpha, beta and gamma are three different kinds of radiation.
rows.explanation: They come out of a changing nucleus, but they are three different things.

rows.statement: Alpha, beta and gamma are just three names for the same thing.
rows.explanation: They are different from each other. That is why they have different names.

rows.statement: Half-life is about a crowd of nuclei, not a timer inside each atom.
rows.explanation: In a big group, half of the unstable nuclei change in one half-life. You cannot say which ones.

rows.statement: After one half-life, all the radioactive nuclei in a sample are gone.
rows.explanation: After one half-life, half of them are left, not none.

rows.statement: In a decay chain, every change makes a different nucleus, and nothing simply vanishes.
rows.explanation: One decay is not always the end. The new nucleus can change again.
